doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

chapter: The Philly Sound and its makers
title: Social commentary, John Whitehead and Black music in the 1970s
summary: Wake Up Everybody and other political songs by McFadden and Whitehead, and MFSB and Teddy Pendergrass at the White House.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Yes if it's attracting that, those delivery system, that's a big tell. They also seem not to be afraid to write social commentary.
Yeah. Like "Wake Up Everybody" with Harold Melvin and —

Well "Wake Up Everybody" was written by my good friend John Whitehead. That was not a Gamble song. That was McFadden and Whitehead. And John Whitehead and I were friends until he died until he got shot here in the city. But he wrote "Ain't No Stopping Us Now" which is another really big, sort of political song. And he wrote "Back Stabbers," that's a really political song. You know? I mean he was a character that kid. He was a real natural talent.
There was no discussion — or was there — about gee, this is, we can't really release this song this is too controversial?

Not for them. They were always on — black music in those days was always on the left anyway. It was never mainstream, you know? It became mainstream, you know, I mean it really did. You know by the middle '70s and the late '70s it was very mainstream to the point where MFSB went and played the White House one time, when Jimmy Carter was president. So you know Teddy Pendergrass playing the White House? You know? I mean singing at the White House? That's a little weird you know, in the '70s.
